subsystems.name: Tether
subsystems.role: the long, tapered load-bearing element that carries the payload and provides the reach.

subsystems.name: Hub and counterweight
subsystems.role: the tether's centre of mass, which orbits like a satellite, and the ballast that balances the two arms.

subsystems.name: Capture interface
subsystems.role: the lower tip hardware that meets the incoming suborbital vehicle.

subsystems.name: Momentum management
subsystems.role: restores the energy and angular momentum that every payload catch removes.

subsystems.name: Control and dynamics
subsystems.role: keeps the tether spinning, stable and phased for the next catch.

subsystems.name: Launch-vehicle interface
subsystems.role: the suborbital vehicle that climbs to the tip, releases the payload and turns back.

buildSteps.title: Fix the design
buildSteps.detail: The radius, taper and spin rate are chosen so the lower tip moves slowly enough at its lowest point for a suborbital vehicle to catch it, and fast enough at the top for the payload to be released near orbital velocity.

buildSteps.title: Make the tether material
buildSteps.detail: High-strength fibres are spun into yarn and braided into a tether with redundant strands and a tapered cross-section — thick at the hub where tension is highest, thin at the tips.

buildSteps.title: Build the hub and deployer
buildSteps.detail: The hub carries the spool, thrusters, solar arrays and avionics, and must deploy the tether without tangling or snagging.

buildSteps.title: Launch and assemble in orbit
buildSteps.detail: The tether is far longer than any rocket fairing, so it is launched as a coiled package or in segments and deployed under controlled tension, or joined piece by piece.

buildSteps.title: Spin up
buildSteps.detail: Electric thrusters and electrodynamic drag work against gravity-gradient forces to spin the tether up to its operating rate and place the orbit.

buildSteps.title: Install the capture hardware
buildSteps.detail: A grapple or catching net is fitted at the lower tip, with beacon, radar and optical aids for the incoming vehicle.

buildSteps.title: Test with inert payloads
buildSteps.detail: Small, expendable masses are caught and released first, to check timing, damping and tether loads before anything valuable is carried.

buildSteps.title: Operate and reboost
buildSteps.detail: Each catch drains momentum from the rotating system, so between catches the hub fires its solar-electric thrusters to restore spin and orbital altitude.

prerequisites.why: the tether holds itself and the payload under tension, so specific strength sets the maximum practical length.
small tethers have been deployed in orbit, but a kilometre-scale spinning tether has never been built.

prerequisites.tech: A reusable suborbital vehicle with precise timing
prerequisites.why: the catch demands a few kilometres per second and arrival at a moving tip within a narrow window.
momentum and altitude must be restored between catches without consuming chemical propellant.
orbital docking autonomy exists, but catching a fast-moving, rotating tip is a new guidance problem.
a long tether presents a large target area and must survive years of impacts and thermal cycling.

pathway.milestone: ground rigs and short orbital tether experiments that deploy, stabilise and cut a tether
pathway.unlocks: confidence in deployment dynamics, materials and electrodynamic reboost.

pathway.milestone: a sub-scale rotating tether in low Earth orbit that catches and releases an inert test mass
pathway.unlocks: proof that tip rendezvous and momentum transfer work in practice.

pathway.milestone: a full-scale skyhook paired with a reusable suborbital vehicle
pathway.unlocks: payloads reaching orbit for a fraction of the rocket velocity otherwise needed.

pathway.milestone: a network of tethers at different orbits, plus high-energy versions for escape trajectories
pathway.unlocks: routine orbital transfer and cheaper departure toward the Moon and beyond.
